column2: Prepared formula can stand at room temperature for up to 2 hours; any leftovers must be thrown away.
Bottles and teats must be washed after every use.
Wash your hands; use water that has been boiled and cooled to about 70 °C.
Check the temperature by dripping some on the inside of your wrist.
Heating in the microwave: it heats unevenly and can burn the mouth.
Respect your baby's fullness cues; don't push them to finish the bottle.
Frequent vomiting, diarrhoea, rash or fussiness after formula.
Not enough wet nappies or not gaining weight.
Vitamin D and iron supplements
In the Ministry of Health programme, vitamin D is recommended for babies in the first year, and iron from 4 months.
Vitamin D is needed for bone development; the amount in breast milk is not enough.
Iron stores fall after 4–6 months; iron deficiency can affect development.
Drop doses and duration are decided by the doctor.
Ask your family doctor when to start supplements and at what dose.
Giving drops at the same time every day makes forgetting less likely; you can set a reminder in the app.
Iron drops can temporarily stain teeth; rinse the mouth with water afterwards.
If you accidentally gave too many drops, call your poison control centre.
If paleness, weakness or poor appetite continue.
Diarrhoea and vomiting
The biggest risk of diarrhoea and vomiting in babies is fluid loss (dehydration).
Breastfed babies naturally have soft, frequent poos; this is not diarrhoea.
Diarrhoea and vomiting are usually caused by viral infections and pass within a few days.
The rotavirus vaccine helps prevent severe diarrhoea.
Keep breastfeeding or giving formula; give smaller amounts more often.
Use oral rehydration solution (ORS) if your doctor recommends it.
Don't give fruit juice or sugary drinks.
Wash your hands well after changing nappies.
Diarrhoea or vomiting in a baby under 6 months.
Signs of dehydration: no wet nappy for more than 6 hours, dry mouth, sunken soft spot, crying without tears.
Bloody or black stools, green vomit, constant vomiting.
High fever, extreme weakness or difficulty waking.
Constipation in babies
How often babies poo varies a lot; hard poo that is difficult to pass suggests constipation.
Breastfed babies sometimes don't poo for a few days; if it is soft, this is usually normal.
Constipation can become more common when starting solids.
Going red and straining while pooing is not constipation on its own.
If your baby has started solids, give water and fibre-rich foods (plums, pears, vegetable purées).
Do bicycle leg movements and tummy massage.
Don't use enemas, suppositories or laxatives without asking a doctor.
Bloody stools, swollen tummy or vomiting.
A newborn not passing any poo in the first 48 hours.
If constipation lasts more than 2 weeks or affects feeding.
Colds, cough and bronchiolitis
Babies may catch many colds a year; the way they breathe is the most important thing to watch.
A blocked nose makes feeding harder for young babies.
Bronchiolitis (mostly RSV) can cause wheezing and fast breathing under 2 years.
Honey must not be given under 1 year, and cough and cold medicines must not be given under 2–6 years unless a doctor recommends them.
Keep the nose clear with saline drops and a nasal aspirator, especially before feeds.
Feed small amounts often; keep track of fluid intake.
Keep the home free of cigarette smoke and well aired.
Wash hands often; don't let sick people kiss the baby.
Chest pulling in below the ribs or between them, flaring nostrils, wheezing.
Blue lips or face, pauses in breathing: call your local emergency number.
Feeding dropping to half, fewer wet nappies.
Fever in a baby under 3 months.
Ear pain and sticky eyes
Middle ear infections and sticky eyes are common in babies; most get better with simple treatment.
Ear infections usually follow a cold; fussiness and ear pulling may be seen.
A blocked tear duct in newborns can cause watering and mild stickiness.
Giving the bottle lying down can increase the risk of ear infection.
Wipe sticky eyes from the inside out with clean cotton wool dipped in boiled and cooled water.
Do the tear duct massage your doctor recommended.
Don't put cotton buds or drops in the ear (unless a doctor recommends it).
Discharge from the ear, high fever or severe fussiness.
Red eye with thick yellow-green discharge; in a newborn it always needs to be checked.
Swelling and redness of the eyelid.
Head shape and tummy time
Babies who sleep on their backs can develop a flat spot on the back of the head; tummy time reduces this.
Positional flattening is harmless and usually improves with position changes.
Tight neck muscles (torticollis) can make a baby always look to the same side.
Give supervised tummy time a few times a day while awake; start short and build up.
Alternate which side your baby's head faces at each sleep (still on their back).
Limit time in car seats and bouncers; carry your baby in your arms.
If your baby always turns their head to the same side and can't turn to the other.
If flattening increases after 4 months or the forehead/ears are asymmetric.
Early closure of the soft spot or a clearly abnormal head shape.
Vaccines protect babies from serious infections; the national schedule is given free at family health centres.
Türkiye's routine schedule starts with hepatitis B at birth and continues at 2, 4, 6, 12 and 18 months and at school age.
Mild fever, fussiness and redness at the injection site after vaccination are normal and pass in 1–2 days.
Delayed vaccines are not restarted; the doctor completes the missing doses.
Keep the vaccination card and the app's vaccine schedule up to date.
Breastfeeding and cuddling soothe your baby after vaccination.
If a fever reducer is needed, ask your doctor about the dose.
Swelling of the face or lips, shortness of breath or widespread rash within minutes of vaccination: emergency.
Inconsolable crying for more than 3 hours, a seizure or high fever after vaccination.
Baby massage
Gentle massage strengthens your bond, soothes your baby and may help some babies sleep.
The best time for massage is when your baby is calm, awake and not just fed.
If your baby cries, turns their head away or stiffens, take a break.
Use a warm room, warm hands and short nails.
Use an unscented plant oil; test it on a small area first.
Start with the legs and move slowly to the tummy (clockwise), chest, arms and back.
A rash or redness on the skin after massage.
If the tummy is swollen and tender, don't massage; ask a doctor.
Using a dummy
A dummy can soothe your baby and using one at sleep time may lower the risk of SIDS; timing matters.
It is recommended not to give a dummy until breastfeeding is established (usually 3–4 weeks).
Long-term use has been linked to ear infections and tooth alignment problems.
Don't dip the dummy in honey or sugar; don't tie it to a string or cord.
Check it regularly; replace it if cracked or worn.
If the dummy falls out after your baby falls asleep, there's no need to put it back.
Plan to wean off it gradually after 1 year.
If white patches (thrush) appear in the mouth.
Development: 1–2 years
Walking, first words and a wish for independence are the highlights of this stage.
By 15–18 months most children walk on their own and say a few words.
By 18 months they understand simple instructions and can point to body parts.
At 2 years they start making two-word sentences, run and throw a ball.
Talk through daily tasks; repeat what your child says and expand on it.
Read a book together every day.
Offer choices ("red or blue?") and give small tasks.
Choose playing together and moving outdoors over screens.
Not walking or having no words at 18 months.
Not making two-word phrases or not understanding instructions at 2 years.
Not making eye contact, not responding to their name, not pointing.

2 years
Development: 3–6 years
In the preschool years, language, imagination, friendships and self-care skills develop quickly.
3 years: 3–4-word sentences, climbing stairs, pretend play.
4 years: telling stories, knowing colours, standing on one foot.
5–6 years: games with simple rules, interest in letters and numbers, dressing themselves.
Play is the most important way to learn; make time for free play.
Help them name their feelings ("you look angry").
Routines (sleep, meals) give a sense of security.
Don't miss eye and hearing screenings.
Speech that can't be understood or no sentences at 3 years.
No interaction with peers at all, repetitive behaviours.
If stuttering lasts more than 6 months or upsets the child.
3 years
4 years
5 years
Speech delay
Speech development varies from child to child, but some signs need early assessment.
Understanding develops before speaking.
Children growing up bilingual may spread their vocabulary across two languages; this is not a delay.
Hearing problems are an important cause of speech delay.
Get down to your child's level when talking and let them see your face.
Use songs, rhymes and picture books.
Try describing rather than asking questions; limit screen time.
No pointing at 12 months, no single words at 16 months, no two-word sentences at 24 months.
Loss of words already learned.
Any doubt about hearing: have a hearing test.
Tantrums
Tantrums are normal in young children who can't yet regulate their feelings, usually between 1 and 4 years.
Tiredness, hunger and overstimulation can trigger tantrums.
During a tantrum a child can't take in reasoning.
Physical punishment and shouting make behaviour worse in the long run.
Stay calm; make sure your child is safe.
When the tantrum passes, name the feeling and offer a hug.
Reduce triggers in advance: regular sleep and meals, warning before transitions.
Notice and praise the behaviour you want.
If tantrums are very frequent, long, or still severe after age 5.
If the child hurts themselves or others.
If breath-holding spells cause fainting, ask a doctor.
Potty training
Readiness signs, not age, guide potty training; most children are ready between 2 and 3 years.
Readiness signs: staying dry for 2 hours, noticing wetness, understanding simple instructions.
Night dryness may come months or even years after daytime dryness.
Constipation makes potty training harder.
Introduce the potty in advance; let your child sit on it.
Suggest sitting on the potty after waking, after meals and before sleep.
Don't scold for accidents; celebrate successes.
Don't start during big changes such as a new sibling or a move.
Burning when weeing, weeing often, or fever.
If daytime wetting continues after 5 years or night wetting after 7 years.
If wetting starts again after a dry period.
Sleep in children
Enough sleep is essential for growth, learning and behaviour.
Recommended: 1–2 years 11–14 hours; 3–5 years 10–13 hours (including naps).
Daytime naps are usually dropped between 3 and 5 years.
Nightmares and night terrors are common in the preschool years.
Keep a calm bedtime routine at the same time every day.
Turn off screens at least 1 hour before bed.
Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and cool.
Comfort after a nightmare; during a night terror don't try to wake them, just keep them safe.
Snoring, pauses in breathing during sleep, sleeping with the mouth open.
Excessive daytime sleepiness or attention problems.
Child nutrition and picky eating
Young children's appetite varies from day to day; picky eating is common at these ages.
It may take 10–15 tries before a new food is accepted.
3 main meals and 1–2 healthy snacks a day suit most children.
After 1 year, daily milk should not exceed about 2 glasses; more can reduce appetite and iron intake.
You decide what is eaten; the child decides how much.
Eat together as a family, without screens.
Don't use sweets as a reward; limit sugary drinks.
Serve small portions; offer a new food together with a favourite one.
Not gaining weight or dropping off the growth curve.
Eating a very limited range of foods, gagging or difficulty swallowing at meals.
Screen time
Too much screen time at an early age can harm language development, sleep and physical activity.
Screens are not recommended under 18–24 months, except for video calls.
For ages 2–5, at most 1 hour a day of age-appropriate content, ideally watched together, is recommended.
A TV on in the background also reduces play and talk.
Set screen-free zones: the dining table and the bedroom.
Watch together and talk about what you watched.
Try not to use screens as a way to calm your child.
Set an example: review your own screen use too.
If limiting screens causes extreme anger, or there are sleep or social problems, see a specialist.
Dental health in children
Baby teeth hold the place for permanent teeth; decay can cause pain and eating problems.
A rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste is recommended up to age 3, and a pea-sized amount from 3 to 6.
Falling asleep with a bottle and frequent sugary snacks increase the risk of decay.
Brush twice a day under adult supervision; children need help until about 7–8.
See the dentist for a check-up every 6 months.
Water is the best drink.
Brown-black spots on teeth, pain, swollen gums.
A broken or knocked-out tooth after a fall: see a dentist right away.
Common childhood infections
In nursery and preschool, children often catch infections; most get better on their own.
Hand, foot and mouth disease, chickenpox, roseola, flu and stomach bugs are common.
Antibiotics don't work against viruses; they should only be used on a doctor's advice.
Flu and other vaccines reduce the risk of serious illness.
Give plenty of fluids and rest; keep an eye on the fever.
Don't send a sick child to nursery until they are better.
Make handwashing a habit.
Shortness of breath, turning blue, seizure, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed: emergency.
Unable to take fluids, clearly less urine.
Fever lasting more than 3 days or worsening general condition.
A new sibling and jealousy
A new sibling can bring the older child anxiety as well as excitement.
Temporary regression (wetting, baby talk) may be seen.
Jealousy is not a sign of lack of love but of fear of losing attention.
Prepare your child before the sibling arrives with books and play.
Spend some time alone with the older child every day, even if brief.
Give age-appropriate small tasks in caring for the baby.
Make big changes (room, nursery) before the birth or a few months after.
If aggressive behaviour continues or the child withdraws noticeably, see a specialist.
Settling into nursery and school
Separation anxiety is natural when starting somewhere new; a consistent goodbye makes settling easier.
Crying and changes in sleep and appetite may happen in the first weeks.
Frequent infections are expected in the first year.
Say a short, confident goodbye; don't sneak away.
Start with short stays in the first days.
Let them take a favourite object from home.
Keep in regular contact with the teacher.
If settling difficulties grow over weeks or the child is constantly unhappy at school.
Pregnancy planning and folic acid
The time before pregnancy is a time to prepare for a healthy pregnancy.
Folic acid is recommended from at least 1 month before pregnancy through the first 3 months; it reduces neural tube defects.
Chronic conditions and medicines should be reviewed before pregnancy.
Checking rubella and other vaccination status is important.
See an obstetrician or your family doctor for a pre-pregnancy check-up.
Stop smoking and drinking; move towards a healthy weight.
Ask your doctor about the folic acid dose (a higher dose may be needed if you are at risk).
If you are not pregnant after 1 year (6 months if over 35) of regular intercourse.
Early, if you have irregular periods, a chronic condition or previous pregnancy losses.
First trimester (weeks 1–13)
In this period when the organs form, nausea, tiredness and breast tenderness are common.
At the first visit, the location and week of the pregnancy are confirmed by ultrasound.
Nuchal translucency measurement and the combined screening test may be done between weeks 11 and 14.
Most miscarriages happen in the first 12 weeks, usually due to chromosomal differences.
Keep taking folic acid; don't take medicines without asking your doctor.
Eat small amounts often; dry crackers may help morning sickness.
Avoid alcohol, smoking and unpasteurised products.
Enter your last period date in the app's pregnancy tracker.
Severe tummy pain, especially on one side (it may be an ectopic pregnancy).
Bleeding, passing clots.
Vomiting so much you can't keep anything down, less urine.
Second trimester (weeks 14–27)
Usually a time of more energy, when you start to feel your baby move.
First movements are usually felt between weeks 18 and 22.
A detailed anomaly scan is done in weeks 18–22.
Screening for gestational diabetes (glucose tolerance test) is recommended in weeks 24–28.
Regular light to moderate exercise (walking, swimming, pregnancy yoga) is beneficial.
Iron and calcium needs increase; plan your diet and supplements with your doctor.
Consider joining antenatal classes.
Bleeding, regular contractions, leaking fluid.
Severe headache, vision problems, sudden swelling of the face or hands.
Fever, burning when weeing.
Third trimester (weeks 28–40)
Your baby gains weight fast; preparing for birth and tracking movements become important.
Back pain, frequent weeing, heartburn and trouble sleeping are common.
Knowing your baby's movement pattern is important; a clear decrease needs to be checked.
Sleeping on your side (especially the left) is recommended in the last months.
Have your hospital bag ready by week 36.
Plan where you will give birth, transport and your support person.
Pay attention to movements at the same times every day.
A clear decrease or stop in your baby's movements: get checked right away.
Leaking fluid, bleeding, regular painful contractions.
